book.title: Pinḳes Khmielniḳ : yizker-bukh nokh der ḥorev-geṿorener Yidisher ḳehile

overview.title: Reading Pinkes Khmielnik: A Jewish Community Remembered
overview.summary: Chmielnik was a Jewish town with religious institutions, schools, political and youth organizations, trades, shops, and family networks. The memorial book follows this community from earlier Jewish life and modern civic activity through German occupation, forced labor, deportation, murder, flight, hiding, and liberation. It also records survivors’ return, aid work, family histories, and memorial practices after the destruction. Exploring the paths below will help readers understand both the community that was destroyed and the people who preserved its memory. [mention_e3ec081a56e985414d9113d3, mention_e2052c505e1e61fe8bc38243, event_candidate_46bf0a596ab8e9e4bec042c5]

paths.title: What kind of Jewish community was Chmielnik?
paths.description: This path reconstructs Chmielnik as a lived community: a place of worship, commerce, skilled work, family life, and local institutions. By the end, readers will see more than a victim population—they will see the social world that Nazi persecution sought to destroy.
paths.question: How did Jewish people build communal life in Chmielnik?

steps.title: A town of commerce and skilled work
steps.summary: The memorial book calls Chmielnik a former trading town serving nearby villages and small towns. Its accounts name shops, bakeries, tanneries, a brewery, a soap and candle factory, and workshops, showing how Jewish livelihoods were woven into the town’s economy. steps.summary: Chmielnik had synagogues and houses of study, including a Great Beit Midrash used by craftsmen; the town is also remembered as having thirteen Hasidic prayer rooms. Accounts of Torah scroll ceremonies, weddings, and communal prayer show religion functioning as both worship and social connection. paths.title: How did Jewish people debate their future?
paths.description: This path follows Zionist, socialist, religious, and youth movements in Chmielnik. It shows how political disagreement and collective organizing were part of ordinary Jewish public life, not merely responses to persecution.
paths.question: What ideas and organizations shaped Chmielnik’s Jewish public sphere?

steps.title: Political and youth organization
steps.summary: The memorial book describes Poale Zion activity, the later emergence of Left Poale Zion, and the formation of Yugnt-Frayhayt in 1926 through the union of youth groups. These organizations organized workers and young people around competing visions of Jewish communal and political life. paths.title: How did German rule dismantle daily life?
paths.description: This path traces the transition from invasion to persecution: attacks on religious spaces, seizure of Jewish men, forced labor, the ghetto, and coercive Jewish administration. It explains how destruction unfolded through escalating measures rather than in one single event.
paths.question: What changed for Chmielnik’s Jews under German occupation?

steps.title: Invasion and attacks on sacred spaces
steps.summary: The memorial book places the Nazi entry into Chmielnik on September 5, 1939, and records the burning of a Beth Midrash shortly afterward. Another testimony says German forces set the Great Synagogue on fire and shot men who fled, turning religious spaces into targets of terror. [event_candidate_aaf528b242a1b971ed156943, event_candidate_7683c218c1d8fb1672eeadca, event_candidate_13b5eccef376a3e5122fa2ad]

paths.title: How was the community destroyed?
paths.description: This path follows the deportations, mass transports, killings, and destruction of Chmielnik’s Jewish population. It also preserves individual experiences that make the scale of the catastrophe humanly comprehensible.
paths.question: What happened to Chmielnik’s Jews during the Holocaust?

steps.title: Deportations from the town
steps.summary: The book describes Jews from Chmielnik and surrounding settlements being assembled before deportation. One testimony reports that about 11,000 people were robbed, driven to Khentshin, loaded into cattle cars, and transported to Treblinka. [mention_3614d13bf089489b94135b66, event_candidate_7654f8c0b66df0ee8258e213]

paths.title: How did people resist, hide, and survive?
paths.description: This path centers on choices made under extreme danger: escape from transports, hiding with Christian families, evading armed groups, and joining military resistance. It presents survival as a chain of risks, relationships, and acts of courage rather than as a simple outcome.
paths.question: How did Chmielnik Jews resist destruction and survive?

steps.title: Escaping transports and camps
steps.summary: The book records escapes from transports into forests and the return of Fredi Podstalska to Chmielnik after she fled a transport. It also names Chmielnik Jews who attempted escape from the Kielce HASAG camp, though some were captured and killed. paths.title: How did Chmielnik survive in memory?
paths.description: This path follows the community after liberation: return, testimony, landsmen aid, family lists, organizations, and monuments. It shows how survivors transformed loss into documentation and communal responsibility.
paths.question: How was the destroyed community remembered and rebuilt after the war?

steps.title: Returning to a changed hometown
steps.summary: After arriving in Poland, one narrator went to Chmielnik, described as his beloved hometown. The return connected liberation with confrontation with the place where family and community life had been destroyed. [event_candidate_065478cb1c27c4376d98b419, mention_b16f50f2824d02676401b5a1]

steps.title: Testimony as preservation
steps.summary: Survivors’ accounts were presented to the Central Jewish Historical Commission in Munich, and the memorial book cites memoirs such as Yosef Kaufman’s account of Hitlerism. steps.summary: Chmielnik landsmen organized relief, including a 1939 dance whose proceeds went to the Joint for Chmielnik and later money sent to the town. After the war, roughly 400 families descended from Chmielnik were recorded in Israel, demonstrating the persistence of communal networks across countries. timeline.summary: German forces entered Chmielnik in September 1939, burned Jewish religious buildings, seized Jewish men, and drove residents into flight. One narrator left the town on November 11, 1939.
